report:
Conclusion: the claim is **supported for adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)**, especially witnessed arrests of presumed cardiac cause. The strongest direct evidence is a JAMA cohort analysis concluding that lay-rescuer **compression-only CPR was associated with increased survival versus both conventional CPR and no bystander CPR** in a system promoting hands-only CPR: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668. A nationwide NEJM study likewise found CPR before EMS arrival was associated with substantially higher 30-day survival than no early CPR: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1405796.

Mechanistically and clinically, this fits AHA guidance: hands-only CPR can start sooner, minimize interruptions, and is recommended for untrained lay rescuers in adult witnessed OHCA: https://web.archive.org/web/20180604124432/http://circ.ahajournals.org/content/117/16/2162. Dispatcher assistance further supports benefit versus no bystander CPR, including neurologically intact survival: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853623/.

Caveats: most evidence is observational, so residual confounding is possible; “greater survival” is an association, not proof for every subgroup. Benefit is clearest for adults with sudden witnessed collapse; conventional CPR with breaths remains important for children and likely asphyxial arrests. Overall, doing hands-only CPR is far better than doing nothing while awaiting EMS.
